summary:
EarthScope is an existing climate dashboard upgraded in place. The project combines a FastAPI service and a single-page HTML/JavaScript interface (Chart.js, deck.gl, and MapLibre) with a normalized SQLite archive of NASA POWER Daily data. The refreshed build adds seven locations to the original cohort, expanding coverage to twelve cities in twelve countries; it also adds coverage, comparison, trend, and 48-series estimate panels and records a reproducible model-evaluation suite.
The archive contains 446,364 daily-variable observations. All 48 location-variable series have zero missing normalized values under the stated qualification rule, with no interpolation. The suite uses chronological model selection, calibration, and held-out test periods. Its metrics and trends are retrospective, descriptive results; they do not establish causation, predict disasters, or constitute operational forecasts or official warnings.

Project details: EarthScope

EarthScope is a web-based tool for exploring environmental change over time. The challenge it addresses is how to select Earth-science variables, visualize how they change, and understand what is changing, where it is changing, and by how much. EarthScope brings data, maps, charts, comparisons, and historical analysis together in one dashboard.

What it does and how it works

Users can choose among four daily variables—air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and corrected precipitation—and explore them for twelve city locations in twelve countries. The project includes a SQLite archive of 446,364 daily-variable observations from NASA POWER, as well as a live-data mode and a clearly labelled simulated demo mode.

The dashboard displays selected data in a map, readings table, and time-series charts. Its archive tools report data coverage and completeness, compare locations over a shared date range, and calculate annual and seasonal summaries. Annual trend slopes are calculated using complete calendar years. The project also includes 48 one-day, archive-origin statistical estimates—one per location and variable—with results evaluated against held-out historical data.

Benefits and intended impact

EarthScope makes a large environmental dataset easier to explore without requiring users to query a database or write analysis code themselves. It helps users compare locations, inspect changes over time, and see data coverage and limitations alongside the results. The intended impact is to support learning and early-stage environmental analysis by making historical data and its interpretation more accessible and transparent.

Tools and technologies

The project was developed using Python for the data processing, analysis, and backend; FastAPI for the API; SQLite for the historical archive; and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser dashboard. It uses NASA POWER Daily data, with MapLibre/deck.gl for map visualization and Chart.js for charts. The model suite uses statistical methods, including ridge regression, and pytest for automated tests. Development and use require a standard computer and web browser; no specialized hardware is needed.

What is creative about the project

EarthScope combines historical data access, comparison, visual exploration, trend summaries, and model evaluation in one application. It also makes data provenance, completeness, and scientific caveats part of the experience rather than presenting results without context. The incident panel provides a demonstration of explainable threshold rules, while explicitly identifying them as prototypes rather than official warnings.

Factors the team considered

The team considered data quality, missing values, units, date alignment, geographic coverage, reproducibility, and how to communicate uncertainty. NASA POWER values are gridded estimates at the selected city coordinates, not station readings or national averages. The trend slopes are descriptive and do not test statistical significance or establish causes. The one-day estimates are not operational weather forecasts and do not predict disasters. Prototype incident levels are not official warnings, and the incident workflow does not contact emergency services.

The current version addresses parts of the challenge—manual selection from four variables, visualization, and location-level descriptive rates of change—but does not yet test trend significance, search a broad catalogue of Earth-science variables, map continuous regional patterns, or identify causal drivers.
